---
title: "Exercise: the pinhole camera and calibration"
---

## Goal

By the end of this exercise you should be able to:

- project a 3D point to a pixel by hand, and turn a pixel back into a ray,
- convert a focal length in millimetres into pixels and compute a field of view,
- say what radial distortion does to a point, and recognise barrel and pincushion,
- count equations and unknowns for the DLT and for planar calibration, and name the degenerate setups,
- read a picture of reprojection residuals: noise, or a missing model term?
- *(math)* derive the DLT equations, the camera centre and the planar calibration constraints.

Do the pen-and-paper part first, then the two demos.

## Background

| Idea | What it means |
|---|---|
| Pinhole | $u = f X/Z + c_x$, $v = f Y/Z + c_y$ in camera coordinates ($z$ forward, $y$ down) |
| Focal length in pixels | focal length / pixel pitch, e.g. 8 mm / 10 µm = 800 px |
| Intrinsics $K$ | $f_x, f_y$, principal point $(c_x, c_y)$, skew; fixed while zoom and focus are fixed |
| Extrinsics | rotation $R$, translation $\mathbf t$: camera coordinates $= R\mathbf X + \mathbf t$; centre $\mathbf c = -R^\top\mathbf t$ |
| Camera matrix | $P = K[R \mid \mathbf t]$, $3 \times 4$, 11 degrees of freedom |
| Pixel → ray | from $\mathbf c$ in the direction $R^\top K^{-1}(u, v, 1)^\top$ |
| Radial distortion | $r \to r(1 + k_1 r^2 + k_2 r^4)$ in normalised coordinates; $k_1 < 0$ barrel, $k_1 > 0$ pincushion |
| DLT | 2 linear equations per point in the 12 entries of $P$; $\ge 6$ points, not all on one plane |
| Homography | image of a plane, $3 \times 3$, 8 degrees of freedom, $\ge 4$ points; planar calibration: 2 equations on $K$ per pose |
| Reprojection error | pixel distance between the seen and the predicted position of a known point |

## By hand

Unless stated otherwise: $f = 800$ px, $(c_x, c_y) = (320, 240)$, no skew, an image of $640 \times 480$ pixels, and the camera at the world origin looking down $+z$ ($R = I$, $\mathbf t = 0$).

**B1.** Project the points $(0.5, -0.25, 5)$, $(0.5, -0.25, 10)$ and $(0.4, 0.3, 2)$ (metres) to pixels. As a point moves away from the camera along a straight line through the camera centre, where does its image go? Which pixel never moves when only $Z$ changes?

**B2.** The pixel $(400, 200)$. (a) Compute $K^{-1}(400, 200, 1)^\top$. (b) Which 3D points land on this pixel? Check that one of your points from B1 is among them.

**B3.** (a) The horizontal and vertical field of view of this camera. (b) A camera has an 8 mm lens and pixels of 3.45 µm. What is $f$ in pixels? (c) With 2 × 2 binning (pixels of 6.9 µm, an image half as wide), what happens to $f$ in pixels and to the field of view?

**B4.** Radial distortion with $k_1 = -0.1$, $k_2 = 0$. (a) A point at normalised radius $r = 0.4$: where does it go? Barrel or pincushion? (b) How many pixels is that with $f = 800$? (c) The same with $k_1 = +0.1$. (d) Why does distortion matter more in the corners of the image than in the centre?

**B5.** Counting. (a) How many equations do 5 points give for the DLT? 6 points? How many unknowns are there? (b) Why do 6 points on one plane not determine $P$, even though there are enough equations? (c) How many points determine a homography? (d) Planar calibration gives 2 equations on $K$ per pose. How many poses are needed for a $K$ with 5 unknowns? With zero skew assumed?

**B6.** Four calibrations, described by their residual arrows (observed → predicted). For each: random noise, or a model problem? Which one?
(a) Arrows in random directions, RMS 0.3 px.
(b) All arrows point radially outwards, longest in the image corners, about 3 px there.
(c) 71 arrows of about 0.3 px in random directions, and one arrow of 12 px.
(d) A second calibration of the same camera after the lens was refocused gives a focal length 2 % larger.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Solutions"}
**B1.** $(0.5, -0.25, 5)$: $u = 800 \cdot 0.5/5 + 320 = 400$, $v = 800 \cdot (-0.25)/5 + 240 = 200$. $(0.5, -0.25, 10)$: $(360, 220)$. $(0.4, 0.3, 2)$: $(480, 360)$. Moving away along a line through the camera centre the image does not move at all (it is the same ray); moving away along a line parallel to the optical axis, as from $Z = 5$ to $Z = 10$ here, the image slides towards the principal point $(320, 240)$, which is the only pixel that never moves.

**B2.** (a) $\big((400 - 320)/800, (200 - 240)/800, 1\big) = (0.1, -0.05, 1)$. (b) All points $s \cdot (0.1, -0.05, 1)$ with $s > 0$ (a ray from the origin). $s = 5$ gives $(0.5, -0.25, 5)$, the first point of B1.

**B3.** (a) Horizontally $2\arctan(320/800) = 43.6°$, vertically $2\arctan(240/800) = 33.4°$. (b) $8\ \text{mm} / 3.45\ \mu\text{m} = 2319$ px. (c) $f$ halves to 1159 px, the image is half as wide in pixels, so the field of view is unchanged: the same sensor and lens see the same scene, only with coarser pixels.

**B4.** (a) $0.4 \cdot (1 - 0.1 \cdot 0.16) = 0.3936$: inwards, barrel. (b) $800 \cdot 0.0064 = 5.1$ px. (c) $0.4 \cdot 1.016 = 0.4064$, outwards: pincushion. (d) The displacement is $k_1 r^3$: it grows with the cube of the distance from the centre, so it is tiny near the centre and largest in the corners.

**B5.** (a) 10 and 12 equations; $P$ has 12 entries but only 11 unknowns (the scale is free), so 5 points are too few and 6 are enough. (b) If all points lie on one plane, the part of $P$ that multiplies the coordinate perpendicular to that plane never appears in the equations: it can be anything, so a whole family of $P$ fits. (c) 4 points (8 equations for 8 unknowns). (d) 3 poses ($3 \cdot 2 = 6 \ge 5$); with zero skew, 4 unknowns, so 2 poses.

**B6.** (a) Noise: a good calibration. (b) A pattern: a radial distortion that the model does not include (or underestimates); add $k_1$. (c) One outlier: a wrongly detected corner; remove it, then the RMS drops to about 0.3 px. (d) A model change: focusing moves the lens and changes the focal length (and distortion); the intrinsics are only fixed while zoom and focus are fixed.
:::

### Math questions

**B7.** *(math)* From $\mathbf x \times P\mathbf X = 0$ with $\mathbf x = (u, v, 1)^\top$ and the rows $\mathbf p_1^\top, \mathbf p_2^\top, \mathbf p_3^\top$ of $P$, derive the two equations of the DLT. Why is the third component of the cross product not a new equation?

**B8.** *(math)* Show that $\mathbf c = -R^\top\mathbf t$ satisfies $P\binom{\mathbf c}{1} = 0$. Why is the centre the only point that does not project to a pixel?

**B9.** *(math)* For a plane at $Z = 0$, show that $H = K[\mathbf r_1\ \mathbf r_2\ \mathbf t]$ and derive the two constraints $\mathbf h_1^\top\omega\,\mathbf h_2 = 0$ and $\mathbf h_1^\top\omega\,\mathbf h_1 = \mathbf h_2^\top\omega\,\mathbf h_2$ with $\omega = K^{-\top}K^{-1}$.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Solutions (math)"}
**B7.** $P\mathbf X = (\mathbf p_1^\top\mathbf X, \mathbf p_2^\top\mathbf X, \mathbf p_3^\top\mathbf X)^\top$. The cross product with $(u, v, 1)$:
$$\begin{pmatrix} v\,\mathbf p_3^\top\mathbf X - \mathbf p_2^\top\mathbf X \\ \mathbf p_1^\top\mathbf X - u\,\mathbf p_3^\top\mathbf X \\ u\,\mathbf p_2^\top\mathbf X - v\,\mathbf p_1^\top\mathbf X \end{pmatrix} = \mathbf 0.$$
The first two rows are linear in $\mathbf p = (\mathbf p_1, \mathbf p_2, \mathbf p_3)$: $[\mathbf 0^\top, -\mathbf X^\top, v\mathbf X^\top]\,\mathbf p = 0$ and $[\mathbf X^\top, \mathbf 0^\top, -u\mathbf X^\top]\,\mathbf p = 0$. The third row is $-u$ times the first minus $v$ times the second, so it adds nothing.

**B8.** $P\binom{\mathbf c}{1} = K(R\mathbf c + \mathbf t) = K(-RR^\top\mathbf t + \mathbf t) = K(-\mathbf t + \mathbf t) = 0$. A point projects to a pixel only if $P\binom{\mathbf X}{1}$ has a non-zero third entry; the zero vector is no pixel at all (it is the "ray of all rays"). $P$ has rank 3, so its null space is one-dimensional: the centre is the only such point.

**B9.** For $\mathbf X = (X, Y, 0, 1)$: $[\mathbf r_1\ \mathbf r_2\ \mathbf r_3\ \mathbf t]\mathbf X = X\mathbf r_1 + Y\mathbf r_2 + \mathbf t = [\mathbf r_1\ \mathbf r_2\ \mathbf t](X, Y, 1)^\top$, so $H \simeq K[\mathbf r_1\ \mathbf r_2\ \mathbf t]$. Hence $\mathbf h_1 = \lambda K\mathbf r_1$, $\mathbf h_2 = \lambda K\mathbf r_2$ with one common factor $\lambda$, i.e. $\mathbf r_k = K^{-1}\mathbf h_k/\lambda$. The columns of a rotation are orthonormal: $\mathbf r_1^\top\mathbf r_2 = 0$ gives $\mathbf h_1^\top K^{-\top}K^{-1}\mathbf h_2 = 0$, and $\mathbf r_1^\top\mathbf r_1 = \mathbf r_2^\top\mathbf r_2$ gives $\mathbf h_1^\top\omega\,\mathbf h_1 = \mathbf h_2^\top\omega\,\mathbf h_2$ ($\lambda^2$ cancels). Both are linear in the 6 entries of the symmetric $\omega$.
:::

## Explore: the pinhole camera {#explore-pinhole}

A scene (a checkerboard floor of 2 m × 2 m, a box, three posts) seen from outside (left, drag to turn) and through the camera (right, 640 × 480 pixels). The camera always looks at the same point of the scene; sliders set the focal length, principal point, skew, its position (azimuth, elevation, distance), roll and distortion. Click a pixel to see its ray in 3D.

```{=html}
<link rel="stylesheet" href="../demos/dist/demo.css">
<div data-demo="pinhole"></div>
<script src="../demos/dist/pinhole.js"></script>
```

**D1.** At the start ($f = 600$ px), read the horizontal field of view. Check it with $2\arctan(320/f)$. Then double $f$: what happens to the field of view and to the image?

**D2.** Compare zooming and walking: set $f = 1200$ (the box gets bigger). Reset, and instead halve the distance. Describe the difference between the two pictures (look at the posts and the far edge of the board).

**D3.** Preset **long lens from far away**: $f = 1500$ px at distance 7.5. The board has about the same size as at the start. What changed? Which situation in microscopy is the preset **nearly orthographic** like?

**D4.** Preset **a point behind the camera** and tick the box. Where do the red crosses appear, and why is it wrong to draw them?

**D5.** Click the pixel $(c_x, c_y)$ (the red circle). Read $K^{-1}(u, v, 1)$. Where does that ray point? Move the principal point with the sliders and click it again.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Solutions"}
**D1.** $2\arctan(320/600) = 56.1°$, as shown. At $f = 1200$: $2\arctan(320/1200) = 29.9°$; the image shows a smaller part of the scene, magnified 2×, without any change in perspective.

**D2.** Zooming scales the whole image: near and far things grow equally, the posts keep their lean. Walking closer makes near things grow more than far things: the near posts become much larger than the far ones and lean outwards more, the board's far edge shrinks relative to the near edge. Perspective depends on where the camera **is**, not on the lens.

**D3.** The perspective flattens: the posts are nearly parallel, near and far squares of the board have almost the same size. That is a telecentric (orthographic) view, as in many microscopes: magnification does not depend on depth, so the camera is affine.

**D4.** Points behind the camera have $Z < 0$; dividing by a negative depth flips them through the principal point to the other side of the image, where they would appear as if in front. Every projection must check $Z > 0$ first (the graphics pipeline clips before the division for the same reason).

**D5.** $K^{-1}(c_x, c_y, 1) = (0, 0, 1)$: straight along the optical axis, wherever the principal point is. Moving the principal point shifts the whole image; the ray of the principal point stays the optical axis.
:::

## Explore: calibrating a camera {#explore}

A hidden camera ($f = 820$ px, principal point $(335, 245)$, $640 \times 480$ pixels) photographs a known target with seeded pixel noise and, optionally, radial distortion. **3D target**: two checkerboard walls at right angles, 72 corners; click corners to leave them out. **Flat board**: 8 × 6 corners in 1–5 poses. **Linear** = the DLT (or homographies → $K$); **refine** = minimise the reprojection error (optionally with $k_1, k_2$). Red arrows: residuals, magnified. The bars are the singular values of the linear system.

```{=html}
<link rel="stylesheet" href="../demos/dist/demo.css">
<div data-demo="dltcalib" data-preset="six"></div>
<script src="../demos/dist/dltcalib.js"></script>
```

**E1.** Preset **6 points, no noise**. Is the estimate exact? Look at the smallest singular value. Now set the noise to 0.5 px (same 6 points). How far off is $f_x$, and what is the RMS reprojection error? Why is a small reprojection error no guarantee here?

**E2.** Preset **noise 0.5 px, all 72 points**. Read $f_x$, $c_x$, $c_y$ and the RMS error. Press **refine ×20**. Does it change much? Compare the RMS with $0.5\sqrt 2$.

**E3.** Preset **unnormalised DLT**. Compare the condition number and the estimate with the normalised one (tick the box). Which matters more here?

**E4.** Preset **all points on one plane**. How many singular values are (nearly) zero? Why can no $K$ be found?

**E5.** Preset **distortion ignored**. Describe the residual pattern. Press **refine ×20** without and then with **refine k1, k2 too**. Compare $f_x$, $c_y$, $k_1$ and the RMS each time.

**E6.** Preset **flat board: 1, 2, 3 views**. Set the number of views to 1, 2, 3 and 5. When does a $K$ appear, and how close is it to the truth? Refine at 3 views.

**E7.** Preset **parallel views**. What happens at 2, 3 and 5 views? Explain with a sentence about focal length and distance.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Solutions"}
**E1.** Exact: $f_x = 820.0$, the twelfth singular value is 0 (an exact null vector). With 0.5 px noise and the same 6 points: $f_x = 759.3$ (60 px off), yet the RMS reprojection error is only 0.25 px. Six points give 12 equations for 11 unknowns, so the model can nearly fit the noise itself; the small residual shows a good fit, not a good camera. Many points spread over the image are needed.

**E2.** Linear: $f_x = 819.7$, $(c_x, c_y) = (332.5, 247.2)$, RMS 0.718 px. After refining: $f_x = 820.1$, RMS 0.720 px (slightly higher, because the refinement holds the skew at 0 while the DLT had a small non-zero skew). $0.5\sqrt 2 = 0.71$: the residuals are as large as the noise, as they should be.

**E3.** Condition number $2.9 \cdot 10^4$ unnormalised against 8.3 normalised; the estimates agree here ($f_x = 819.6$ against 819.7), because double precision copes with $10^4$. The conditioning matters for larger images, more noise, or single-precision arithmetic; normalising costs nothing, so always do it.

**E4.** Three are zero, and a fourth is small (it would be zero without noise): the columns of $P$ that multiply the coordinate perpendicular to the plane are undetermined. Any $P$ in a 4-dimensional family fits, so no meaningful $K$ can be extracted (the table shows nonsense or nothing).

**E5.** The arrows form a radial pattern, growing towards the edges. Linear: $f_x = 954.7$, $c_y = 300.6$, RMS 1.08 px. Refined without distortion: $f_x = 957.2$, RMS 1.08 px: the pinhole model cannot explain bent lines, so it compensates with a wrong focal length. With $k_1, k_2$: $f_x = 819.8$, $c_y = 250.8$, $k_1 = -0.275$ (true $-0.3$), RMS 0.43 px ($\approx 0.3\sqrt 2$).

**E6.** 1 view: only 3 equations for 5 unknowns (with the zero-skew row): no $K$. 2 views: $f_x = 840$ (zero skew assumed). 3 views: $f_x = 832.6$, and 833.3 after refinement; 5 views: 830.2. Within about 2 % of 820: with 0.5 px noise and moderate tilts, the focal length of a planar calibration is uncertain by about that much; more and more strongly tilted views help.

**E7.** 2 views: $f_x \approx 3100$; 3 views: no valid $K$ at all; 5 views: $f_x \approx 7300$. Seen face-on, a board at distance $Z$ photographed with focal length $f$ looks the same as one at $2Z$ with $2f$: the images cannot separate $f$ from the distance. Tilting the board breaks the tie, because foreshortening depends on $f$.
:::

## Where this leads

The calibrated camera turns pixels into rays. The next unit takes **two** cameras: a point in one image constrains its match in the other to a **line**, and two matched rays give a 3D point. The reprojection error comes back as the objective of **bundle adjustment**, which refines many cameras and thousands of points at once.
